items.readable_text:
Content:
When we graph a function, the range is the set of all [MATH: y]-values given by the graph.

Content:
For example, consider the linear function [MATH: f(x) = 2x,] graphed below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dc679878b825da6990708130270b7280]

Content:
The graph covers all [MATH: y]-values, so the range of the function is

Content:
[MATH: -\infty < y< \infty,]

Content:
which we can also write as
[MATH: -\infty < f(x) < \infty.]

Content:
Furthermore, we can express the range as [MATH: f(x)\in (-\infty,\infty)] using interval notation.

Content:
If we restrict the domain, the range also changes. Let's now consider the function
[MATH: g(x) = 2x, \quad x \in [0,2).]

Content:
The graph [MATH: y = g(x)] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/056bbb68097676bf0f5810553a25350d]

Content:
The [MATH: y] values go from [MATH: y=0] up to (but not including) [MATH: y=4,] including every value in between. Therefore, the range of the function is

Content:
[MATH: 0\leq g(x) < 4.]

Content:
Using interval notation, we can also write the range as [MATH: g(x)\in [0,4).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The range of a function is the collection of numbers (or set) containing all the function's outputs.

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x),] defined by the mapping diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/aee04da4eb03643b8b5a1cb7b41e27a8]

Content:
In a mapping diagram, the range consists of all the outputs to which an arrow is drawn. Therefore, the range is

Content:
[MATH: \{ -1,2,3 \}.]

Content:
The value [MATH: y=0] is not part of the range because there is no [MATH: x]-value such that [MATH: f(x) = 0.]

---

Item 8 — Tutorial: Graphs of Functions

Content:
When we graph a function, the range is the set of all [MATH: y]-values given by the graph.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dc679878b825da6990708130270b7280]

Content:
The graph covers all [MATH: y]-values, so the range of the function is

Content:
[MATH: -\infty < y< \infty,]

Content:
which we can also write as
[MATH: -\infty < f(x) < \infty.]

Content:
Furthermore, we can express the range as [MATH: f(x)\in (-\infty,\infty)] using interval notation.

Content:
If we restrict the domain, the range also changes. Let's now consider the function

Content:
[MATH: 0\leq g(x) < 4.]

Content:
Using interval notation, we can also write the range as [MATH: g(x)\in [0,4).]
